College laptops don’t have to be embarrassing. Nor do they have to be overly expensive. There are a lot of great, well-designed laptops for college students that combine long battery life, easy portability, and the performance needed for everyday coursework.

In my decade-plus of reviewing laptops, I’ve tested hundreds of models. If someone asked me what to buy for a college student, these are the ones I’d suggest.

Be sure to check out our other computing guides, including the [Best Laptops](https://www.wired.com/gallery/best-laptops/), [Best Budget Laptops](https://www.wired.com/gallery/best-cheap-laptops/), [Best MacBooks](https://www.wired.com/story/which-macbook-should-you-buy/), [Best Windows Laptops](https://www.wired.com/gallery/best-windows-laptops/), [Best Gaming Laptops](https://www.wired.com/gallery/best-gaming-laptops/), [Best Chromebooks](https://www.wired.com/gallery/best-chromebooks/), and [Best Laptop Bags](https://www.wired.com/gallery/the-best-backpacks-for-work/).

_Updated July 2026: I’ve added the HP OmniBook 3 and Dell 14 Plus as picks, and the Dell 14S as an honorable mention. I’ve also removed some options that have become too expensive after price increases._

The [MacBook Air](https://www.wired.com/review/macbook-air-m5/) (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is my choice for [best overall laptop](https://www.wired.com/story/best-laptops/) for everyone. But college students have specific needs—and often, specific budgets. In addition to being affordable, a college student’s laptop should be lightweight and easy to carry around. The [MacBook Neo](https://www.wired.com/review/apple-macbook-neo/) (7/10, WIRED Recommends) fits the bill perfectly. It’s only 2.7 pounds and starts at just $699. It also has a smaller display, which helps it fit on those tiny lecture-hall desks. What makes the MacBook Neo special, however, is its lack of compromise around quality. It’s a gorgeous piece of hardware, with fun colors, an excellent trackpad, a beautiful display, and that Apple “it” factor. I recommend the $699 model, which gets you twice the storage and a Touch ID fingerprint reader.

Of course, this isn’t a laptop without downsides. Apple invested its efforts in the front-of-screen experience, but made cuts to performance, ports, and memory to keep costs low. The limitation of 8 GB of memory is my biggest sticking point with this device; it means you’ll need to be mindful of how many applications, tabs, and background tasks you have running at once. Also, ghe Neo can connect to only one external display at a time.

Laptop pricing has skyrocketed over the past few months, which has made it harder to recommend some of the flashier new laptops of the year. Fortunately, many really great laptops from 2025 are still available to buy. The Dell 14 Plus is a great example. It’s one of the few laptops you can get for less than $1,000 that doesn’t force you to make serious compromises. It’s not the world’s prettiest device, but the display is surprisingly sharp, bright, and colorful. The computer’s touchpad and keyboard are both high-quality, and it has tons of ports.

The newer [Dell 14S](https://www.wired.com/review/dell-14s/) came out more recently with the intention to replace the 14 Plus. The new model comes with an OLED display and superb battery life. While it’s a solid option (see Other Laptops to Consider, below), [it starts at a pricey $1,350](https://cna.st/affiliate-), and the screen has a lower resolution. For a college student, the Dell 14 Plus is the better buy right now.

If the idea of buying a laptop with only 8 GB of RAM in 2026 seems questionable (I don’t blame you for feeling this way), I recommend the [Asus Zenbook A14](https://www.wired.com/review/asus-zenbook-a14/) (WIRED Recommends, 8/10). Not only does it come with 16 GB of RAM, but it’s the lightest laptop you can buy right now at just 2.4 pounds. You’ll hardly notice it in [your laptop bag](https://www.wired.com/gallery/the-best-backpacks-for-work/) when you’re trekking across campus.

The price of the Zenbook A14 varies quite a bit, typically between $600 and $1,000, but there’s often a deal available that makes it an affordable option. There’s also the [2026 model](https://cna.st/affiliate-), which comes with the [second-gen Snapdragon X2 chip](https://www.wired.com/story/qualcomm-snapdragon-x2-chips-2025/). At $1,600, though, it’s just not worth the extra cash—especially for a college student on a budget.

The options listed above are fairly affordable, all coming in at less than $1,000. But even if your budget is $600 or less, trust that you can still get a solidly performing laptop with good battery life. The [HP OmniBook 5 frequently sells](https://cna.st/affiliate-) for around $600 or less, making it an adequate MacBook Neo alternative. Better yet, HP’s laptop ships with more memory and storage. The OLED panel display is fantastic too, and the laptop is remarkably thin. The only significant downside is the touchpad, which feels clumsy to use. I could get used to it over time, but it is the Achilles’ heel of this OmniBook 5 (and nearly all [budget laptops](https://www.wired.com/gallery/best-cheap-laptops/), for that matter).

If you need a super-cheap Windows laptop, though, there’s really only one I’d recommend that’s cheaper than the OmniBook 5, and it comes from the same family. I tested the HP OmniBook 3 and found that it shares a lot of the positive qualities of its older sibling. The OLED screen is great, as is the keyboard and overall build quality. Most important, the battery life is top-notch for a device of this price. It’s not as thin as the OmniBook 5 though, and the 1920 x 1200 resolution stretched across the 16-inch screen is unfortunate. There’s also [a 14-inch version](https://cna.st/affiliate-), which I think is a smarter buy.

But there’s not a single other Windows laptop I’d feel good about suggesting someone buy at this price. Intel-powered laptops at this price tend to struggle with performance and battery life, while other cheap Qualcomm Snapdragon X laptops like the [Asus Vivobook 14](https://cna.st/affiliate-) use terrible displays to drag the prices down.

[Chromebooks](https://www.wired.com/story/best-chromebooks/) are becoming increasingly tough to sell. Snapdragon X-powered laptops like the HP OmniBook 3 above have made budget-tier Chromebooks, with weak battery life and poor screens, harder to justify. Furthermore, Chromebooks have the added problem of incompatibility with certain software you might need in college.

However, Chromebooks are still the way to go if you need something— _anything_—for as little money as possible. If you’re low on cash and just need basic internet access, the $200 Asus Chromebook CX15 is your best bet. The screen and touchpad are the main downfalls, but it’s fairly portable and modern-looking, and the battery life is decent enough. My bar is fairly low for a $200 laptop, but the CX15 outdoes other competitors at this price.

Not everyone needs a powerful laptop to tote around campus. But if you’re in a STEM field, or even just like to play games on the weekend, buying a single, powerful laptop to serve as your main machine at college is a good idea. Unfortunately, no gaming laptop is powerful, portable, and affordable—you can only have two of those three things. Letting go of the portability priority, the best option I’ve tested is the [Lenovo LOQ 15](https://www.wired.com/review/lenovo-loq-15/) (8/10, WIRED Recommends). It’s hard to beat a discrete graphics processing unit (GPU) for raw performance, which is exactly what the RTX 5060 in the LOQ 15 delivers. Though the price often creeps above $1,000, it’s still the most affordable gaming laptop you can buy that doesn’t suffer from severe performance compromises.

[![Front view of Razer Blade 16 2025 edition, a slim black laptop, with abstract art on the screen](https://media.wired.com/photos/67e5bd328eceed9f2cae96f3/4:3/w_640%2Cc_limit/Razer-Blade-16-2025-Laptop-(front)-Reviewer-Photo-SOURCE-Luke-Larsen.jpg)](https://cna.)

Despite the thin profile of the [Razer Blade 16](https://www.wired.com/review/razer-blade-16-2025/) (8/10 WIRED Recommends), you can configure it with up to an RTX 5090 graphics card. Aside from the compromise of a high price, battery life is a limitation. You might run out halfway through your day, forcing you to find an outlet in a hurry. If you happen to need performance for gaming on the weekends in addition to your schoolwork, the Razer Blade 16 is expensive but totally worth it. I prefer the smaller [Razer Blade 14](https://www.wired.com/review/razer-blade-14-2025/) as a college laptop, but it’s no longer available to purchase right now.

The MacBook Pro, whether you opt for the M5 Pro, [M5 Max](https://www.wired.com/review/macbook-pro-16-inch-m5-max/), or an older chip, resolves the issue of battery life. Gaming isn’t its strongest capability, but it delivers exceptional performance in creative applications and can be equipped with up to 128 GB of unified memory for serious on-device AI workloads.

It’s an [expensive accessory](https://www.wired.com/gallery/best-ipad-accessories/), but the keyboard and trackpad are both top-notch, on par with a high-end laptop.

[**Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x for $1,075**](https://cna.st/affiliate-): When it launched, this well-rounded, 15-inch laptop was selling for just $850. These days, it’s a few hundred dollars more, which is why I dropped it from a top pick to an honorable mention. The screen is brighter and more colorful than I expected, and even the touchpad feels smooth and responsive. It even gets excellent battery life and delivers a good balance between screen size and portability.

Photograph: Luke Larsen

**[Microsoft Surface Pro 12 for $750](https://cna.st/affiliate-):** I can’t think of a better device to bring to class for note-taking than the [Surface Pro 12](https://www.wired.com/review/microsoft-surface-pro-12-2025/) (6/10, WIRED Recommends). While I recommend [the larger Surface Pro 13 for most people](https://www.wired.com/story/microsoft-surface-buying-guide/), college students are the exception. The thinner and lighter size of the Surface Pro 12 gives you a super-portable Windows device. It has really solid hardware too. The Snapdragon X Plus provides just as much power and long-lasting battery life as the larger model. I wish it were a bit more affordable, as you’ll still need to add on the [Surface keyboard](https://cna.st/affiliate-) and a USB-C power supply.

[**Framework Laptop 12 for $549**](https://cna.st/affiliate-): You can’t expect most budget laptops to last longer than four years of college. The [Framework Laptop 12](https://www.wired.com/review/framework-laptop-12/) (7/10, WIRED Recommends) promises something longer-lasting, as all Framework laptops do. This one is the smallest and cheapest in the lineup, and despite the price, the display and trackpad are both better than I expected. The only problem is the limited RAM.

Do You Need a Laptop for College?

AccordionItemContainerButton
LargeChevron

Yes. Or, at the very least, some type of computing device you’re comfortable using. A laptop is still the preferred recommendation, but you could alternatively use a desktop in your dorm room paired with an iPad or a note-taking device in class.

The mobile aspect of a laptop makes it extremely easy to take your work with you between classes, while studying in coffee shops or typing notes in lecture, for example. Additionally, a laptop makes it easy to save space in cramped dorm rooms.

But as seen in my recommendations above, devices like the iPad Air and Surface Pro 12 could also be good solutions, as long as you pair them with their respective keyboard accessories.

What Kind of Laptop Is Best for College?

AccordionItemContainerButton
LargeChevron

All our guidelines for [choosing a laptop](https://www.wired.com/story/how-to-buy-the-right-laptop-for-you/) also apply to college laptops, including evaluating the quality of the display and chassis, along with ensuring that the device is fast enough for your work. There are, however, a couple of important considerations specific to college. Portability and battery life are paramount. Regardless of your budget, you want something that will last throughout the day and won't weigh you down while you carry it from class to class. Anything more than 4 pounds will start to feel noticeable in your backpack.

Overall dimensions are important, too. Bringing a 16-inch laptop to class can feel obtuse, given the size of small desks. The same is true if you plan on bringing your laptop to a crowded coffee shop or library. That’s why 13- or 14-inch laptops are preferred. There are even 14-inch gaming laptops, such as the Razer Blade 14, that provide the discrete GPU performance you need without sacrificing portability.

Here are some other specs to consider:

Processor

- **Windows**: If you’re getting a Windows machine, your main options for the processor are Intel or Qualcomm. Both have strengths and weaknesses, but getting a Snapdragon X laptop ensures that you get really solid battery life. See our full guide to [buying a laptop](https://www.wired.com/story/how-to-buy-the-right-laptop-for-you/) for more info.
- **Chromebooks**: These browser-based machines use half a dozen processors, most of which you’ve probably never heard of. There’s a reason for that: Those processors are slow. My recommendation when buying a Chromebook is to stick with a [Chromebook Plus machine](https://www.wired.com/story/google-brings-gemini-to-chrome-os-and-chromebooks/). This is a new standard Google created to ensure a certain level of performance and polish.
- **MacOS**: Apple has been making its own processors for a few years, like the latest M5 chip found inside the latest MacBook Pro. These more powerful MacBook Pros feature integrated GPUs that aim to be comparable with the discrete GPUs you find in Windows laptops. Our [MacBook buying guide](https://www.wired.com/story/which-macbook-should-you-buy/) can help further.

RAM and Storage

Regardless of which OS you choose, the minimum amount of RAM you want in your laptop is 8 GB. That’s enough memory to keep your computer feeling snappy even if it’s running under load. But these days 16 GB is standard, and you’ll find lots of laptops around $800 or less that come with 16 GB. So, if you can afford it—especially if you plan to edit photos or videos as part of your coursework—go for a 16-GB or even 32-GB model.

The new default for storage is 256 GB, and it’ll do if you’re trying to save money. You can always use external storage if you need to add on. Spring for 512 GB or a terabyte if you can, though.

Screen

Screens vary tremendously, but don’t settle for anything less than 1080p (or 1200p for 16:10 aspect ratio displays). For a 13-inch laptop, 1080p is sharp enough. If you’re going with a bigger laptop, 2.5K or even 4K screens will improve the viewing experience. If you’re trying to play games as well, be sure to get something with a higher refresh rate— [120 Hz or 144 Hz](https://www.wired.com/story/high-refresh-rate-explained/) will more than satisfy.

Weight and Battery

Don’t forget you’ll be lugging this thing around. It may be tugging on your back for eight hours or more. At the end of a long day of walking, you will likely notice the difference between a 3-pound and 4-pound laptop. Trust me. Also, consider [picking out a nice bag](https://www.wired.com/gallery/the-best-backpacks-for-work/) to carry your computer in.

Similarly, battery life is very important when you’re (potentially) away from a wall outlet for extended periods. Whatever you end up getting, make sure it’s capable of lasting at least eight hours under real-world use—browsing the web, editing documents, writing emails, and taking notes. Even then, you might want to [consider a portable battery charger](https://www.wired.com/gallery/best-portable-chargers-power-banks/).

Are Chromebooks a Good Option for College?

AccordionItemContainerButton
LargeChevron

Yes, for most college students, Chromebooks are a good option. They are cheaper than MacBooks or Windows laptops, and the Chromebook Plus models offer reliable performance at an affordable price. If your budget is $500 or less, things can get more iffy, but I’ve tested a couple of good options that I recommend in this guide in that price range.

Furthermore, you can run almost all apps in the web these days (including Office 365), and Android apps do a good job of filling in the gaps. Occasionally, though, you may run into some compatibility problems, whether with software or hardware. If you’re in a STEM, art, or design program, however, a Chromebook is probably not a good fit. For example, if you’re required to use CAD or Photoshop, you’ll want a Windows laptop.
